A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSQ research, with matching authors, methods, and principal experiments. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 16 LLMs, including deception scores, temperature and difficulty-ratio ablations, reasoning-trace analyses, and embedding visualizations.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds results comparing benign and incentivizing prompts and analyzing responses to rephrased questions.

M1.justification: The CSQ construction, paired questions, reverse-question bias correction, and intention and behavior metrics remain substantively unchanged. The incentivizing-prompt experiment applies the existing framework under another input condition.

E1.justification: Section 5.4 adds an incentivizing-prompt scenario for GPT-4o and gemma-2-9b-it, extending evaluation beyond benign prompts while retaining the contact-reachability task. Appendix G discusses mathematics, science, and coding as future extensions, without evaluating those domains.

E2.justification: The evaluated model roster remains unchanged. New Table 5 compares benchmark properties descriptively; it does not report experiments evaluating those benchmarks or methods against CSQ.

E3.justification: Section 5.4 introduces a controlled comparison using a fixed sycophantic prefix. Figure 6a also changes its stated aggregation interval from [2,80] to [3,80], although the aggregation formula still starts at 2. The existing question budgets, model versions, temperature, and k setting remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 5.4 adds prompt-sensitivity evidence, and Appendix D.3 adds an analysis of answer variability across rephrased questions, displayed in Figure 15. The temperature and k ablations, repetition control, reasoning-trace studies, and embedding analyses were already present in v2.

E5.justification: v2 already displays uncertainty bands and identifies 95% confidence intervals in Figure 10. v3 Appendix D.3 newly specifies bootstrapping and states that all main evaluation metrics have 95% confidence intervals. This expands statistical documentation without establishing additional runs or seeds.

E6.justification: v3 adds prompt-condition results in Figure 7 and answer-ratio results in Figure 15. Figure 6a changes Spearman correlation from 0.715 to 0.691, mean intention from 0.216 to 0.205, and mean behavior from 0.155 to 0.154, alongside its changed stated interval. Sections 5.3 and C.3 correct model-category assignments and the textual model-size trend. Most existing plots and Tables 1–4 remain unchanged; these revisions do not establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, substantive assumptions, bias-correction formulas, aggregation formula, and sampling construction are retained. Task-symbol corrections in Definition 3.3 and equation renumbering do not change the mathematics. No new proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same principal claims: CSQ evaluates benign-prompt deception, scores generally increase with difficulty and correlate, and greater model capacity does not consistently reduce deception. The added experiments support or extend applications without redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C.3 replaces the assertion that deception increases with model size with an interpretation of generally improving honesty, consistent with the retained downward plots, while qualifying the weak fits and uncertain training-related causes. Section 5.4 adds an interpretation separating sycophancy's effects on intention and behavior. Appendix D.2 explains the sensitivity–discriminability tradeoff in choosing k, and new Appendix G identifies prior knowledge as a substantive obstacle to domain transfer.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-release statement and repository link, and specifies name generation using 100 common first and last names with duplicate removal. It also supplies the exact incentivizing prefix. Existing API, model-version, and hyperparameter disclosures remain; the data-category description moves from Appendix A to Section 5.1.

R1.justification: New Appendix H and Table 5 substantially expand positioning across bias, hallucination, and deception benchmarks, including CrowS-Pairs, TruthfulQA, HaluEval, and game-based studies. Numerous references and a benchmark taxonomy are added, emphasizing performance asymmetry, self-consistency, and benign prompts as distinguishing properties of CSQ.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted rewrites in the introduction, metric motivation, experimental narrative, and conclusion, and moves data preparation into the main experimental setup. It adds explanatory sections and reproducibility and acknowledgment statements, while retaining the main section sequence and much of the existing prose.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 7 and 15 and Table 5, and redraws Figure 6a with swapped score axes and revised labels and legend. It also corrects the behavior-score caption of v2 Figure 8, now Figure 9. Most existing visual content is retained with relocation and renumbering rather than redesign.

improvement.justification: v3 improves reproducibility documentation, adds a useful prompt-condition control, and corrects the model-size and hallucination-versus-guessing interpretations. Its expanded discussion also makes applicability limits clearer. These gains are limited: the new evidence does not independently establish the central inference of deceptive intent, and Section 5.3 still states r > 0.7 despite Figure 6a now reporting 0.691.
